drafts.title: Advent with the Fathers starts November 29
drafts.subtitle: Twenty-six free daily readings, and a book to begin with
drafts.body:
Dear friends,

Advent begins on Sunday, November 29. For the twenty-six days that follow, through Christmas Eve, Bibliotheca Catholica will send one short reading each morning from the Fathers and other public-domain voices in our library: Clement of Rome, Augustine, Catherine of Siena, Thomas à Kempis, Bede, Newman, Thérèse, and more. Each note is brief. Each one links back to the full text on the site, so you can read as little or as much as the day allows.

The plan is already live on the library:

The Advent 2026 reading plan: https://bibliothecacatholica.com/reading/advent-2026/

If you are not yet subscribed here, this is the place to be for those daily notes. They are free, and they always will be. The first weeks look toward Christ's coming at the end of time; from December 17 the readings follow the O Antiphons toward Christmas.

Featured book: Confessions

Among the Advent books, Augustine's Confessions opens the season with a longing many of us know too well in December: a heart that will not settle. Day 3 of the plan (Tuesday, December 1) begins at the famous opening of Book I. You need not wait for that morning. The whole work is free to read on the site now, in the Pusey translation we host.

Read Confessions free: https://bibliothecacatholica.com/work/confessions/

Prefer a print copy? [BOOKSHOP LINK – pending affiliate verification]

Some links are affiliate links; if you buy through them, the library earns a small commission at no extra cost to you.

Great art Thou, O Lord, and greatly to be praised; great is Thy power, and Thy wisdom infinite. … Thou awakest us to delight in Thy praise; for Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee. (St. Augustine, Confessions, Book I, ch. 1; trans. E. B. Pusey (Project Gutenberg #3296; hosted on the site))

That restlessness is not a December problem to fix with more activity. It is the ache of a heart made for God. The Child we wait for is the answer Augustine names: faith given "through the Incarnation of Thy Son."

What to expect

  • Daily, Nov 29 – Dec 24: one short excerpt, a plain reflection, and links to the day's passage and the work page.
  • After Christmas: a weekly From the Library digest on Saturday mornings, with Book of the Week on Wednesdays (web only), then a January Read-Along in Orthodoxy, and the Confessions again for Lent (Ash Wednesday is February 10, 2027).

Save the Advent plan, subscribe if you have not, and, if you like, open Book I of the Confessions before the first candle is lit. We will walk the rest of the way together.

drafts.title: Why Would a Christian Read the Pagans?
drafts.subtitle: Augustine, the gold of Egypt, and the freedom to learn from anyone who tells the truth
drafts.body:
Somewhere in nearly every Catholic library sits a shelf of books by men who never heard of Christ. Plato, Aristotle, Cicero, Virgil. A reader who has just come to the Faith, or come back to it, may reasonably ask what those books are doing there. If we have the Gospels, the Fathers, and the saints, why spend our few reading hours on authors who worshipped idols, or worshipped nothing?

The question is old. Christians were asking it within a few generations of the apostles, and they did not all give the same answer. Looking at how the early Church argued it out is still the best way to answer it for ourselves.

Two answers from the early centuries

Around the year 200, Tertullian of Carthage put the case against in a sentence that has never stopped being quoted:

What indeed has Athens to do with Jerusalem? What concord is there between the Academy and the Church? What between heretics and Christians?

— Tertullian, The Prescription Against Heretics, ch. 7

Tertullian was not being lazy. He was a learned man writing against heretics who had, in his view, built their errors out of borrowed philosophy. He had watched clever arguments carry people away from the creed, and he wanted a wall.

Half a century earlier, St. Justin Martyr had answered the other way. Justin had been a philosopher before he was a Christian, and he did not think his conversion required him to call everything he had learned worthless. In his Second Apology he wrote:

Whatever things were rightly said among all men, are the property of us Christians.

— St. Justin Martyr, Second Apology, ch. 13

Justin's reason is theological, not sentimental. The pagan writers, he says, "spoke well in proportion to the share he had of the spermatic word," the seed of the Word who would become flesh in Christ. What they saw, they saw "darkly." But it was real, and it belonged to the One who gave it.

So the tension is there from the start. One side fears contamination; the other sees scattered seeds of the truth. Both are trying to protect the same thing.

Augustine's turn

St. Augustine knew both instincts from the inside. In the Confessions he tells us that the book which first turned his heart toward God was not Scripture but a lost dialogue of Cicero, the Hortensius. He read it at nineteen, as a student of rhetoric:

But this book altered my affections, and turned my prayers to Thyself O Lord; and made me have other purposes and desires.

— St. Augustine, Confessions, Book III

Later, in the books of the Platonists, he found ideas about God and the soul that helped free him from the materialism that had held him for years. He is careful to say what those books lacked: the Incarnation, the humility of the cross, the grace that heals. But he does not pretend they gave him nothing.

When he became a bishop and sat down to write a handbook for Christian teachers, On Christian Doctrine, he had to decide what to tell young men who would preach and interpret Scripture. Should they read the pagans? His answer became one of the most influential passages on the subject in Christian history. He starts from a principle:

Nay, but let every good and true Christian understand that wherever truth may be found, it belongs to his Master.

— St. Augustine, On Christian Doctrine, Book II, ch. 18

Then, a few chapters later, he gives the image that the whole tradition would remember. When the Israelites left Egypt, God told them to take the Egyptians' gold and silver with them. Augustine reads this as a figure of what Christians should do with pagan learning:

Now these are, so to speak, their gold and silver, which they did not create themselves, but dug out of the mines of God's providence which are everywhere scattered abroad.

— St. Augustine, On Christian Doctrine, Book II, ch. 40

The phrase to notice is "which they did not create themselves." For Augustine, the truth in Plato was never Plato's property in the first place. It came out of God's mine. Reading it is not a raid on enemy territory; it is a recovery of what was always the Lord's.

(We will look more closely at the image itself, and at the Exodus story behind it, in this week's short exploration, "What Did Augustine Mean by the Gold of Egypt?")

The conditions Augustine attached

It would be easy to stop there and conclude that a Christian may read anything. Augustine does not stop there.

First, he distinguishes. Pagan learning contains "false and superstitious fancies and heavy burdens of unnecessary toil," which the Christian "ought to abhor and avoid," as well as "liberal instruction" and "some most excellent precepts of morality." The gold is real, and so are the idols. The reader has to tell them apart.

Second, he warns about the reader's own heart. Immediately after the gold of Egypt, he turns to St. Paul: "Knowledge puffs up, but charity edifies" (1 Cor. 8:1). Whatever riches a student brings out of Egypt, Augustine says, "unless he has kept the passover, he cannot be safe." Learning without humility is not a gain.

Third, he keeps the proportions straight. All the useful knowledge in the pagan books, he says, is poor next to Scripture, "just as poor as the store of gold and silver and garments which the people of Israel brought with them out of Egypt was in comparison with the riches which they afterwards attained at Jerusalem."

So Augustine's answer is neither Tertullian's wall nor an open door. It is a door with a threshold: read freely, discern carefully, stay humble, and keep the Scriptures at the center.

Why this still matters

Few of us are tempted to worship Jupiter. But the question has not gone away. It only changes shape. A Catholic today reads novelists who reject the Faith, historians who doubt the Gospels, philosophers who deny the soul. Our children read them in school. The question "should a Christian read the pagans?" becomes "should I read this book by someone who does not share my faith?"

Augustine gives us more than permission. He gives us a way of reading. We come to a book expecting that, if it contains any truth, that truth is God's and can be received with gratitude. We come knowing that it may also contain errors, which we are free to set down. And we come asking whether the reading is making us more charitable or only more clever.

That last test is the hardest. Augustine's own story shows why it matters. The Hortensius lit a fire in him, but it took years, and a great deal of grace, before that fire found its true object.

St. Thomas Aquinas, eight centuries later, would put the principle in his own terms. Sacred doctrine, he wrote, "makes use also of the authority of philosophers in those questions in which they were able to know the truth by natural reason," but treats those authorities "as extrinsic and probable arguments," not as proof of the Faith. The Christian reader learns from the philosopher without making him a prophet.

What the Church teaches, and what this essay argues

It is worth being clear about which parts of this are the Church's teaching and which are one reader's reflection.

Church teaching. The Church teaches that faith and reason come from the same God and cannot truly contradict each other, and that human reason, even without revelation, can come to know real truths about the world and about God. St. John Paul II developed this at length in his encyclical Fides et Ratio (1998), which is available in the library and repays a slow reading.

The Fathers' counsel. The "gold of Egypt" reading of Exodus is Augustine's interpretation, offered (as he himself says) "without prejudice to any other interpretation that may be as good, or better." It became widely shared, but it is a Father's counsel, not a definition of faith.

This essay's argument. The suggestion that Augustine's three conditions (discernment, humility, and the primacy of Scripture) are a practical guide for reading today is my own application, offered for your consideration and correction.

Where to start

If you would like to read the sources yourself, begin with Book II, chapters 18 to 42 of On Christian Doctrine. It is about an hour of reading, plain, and more practical than you might expect. Then read Book III of the Confessions for the Hortensius, and Book VII for the books of the Platonists. Justin's Second Apology takes less than an hour.

This week's Book of the Week looks at On Christian Doctrine as a whole: what it is for, and where to begin.

drafts.title: Book of the Week: On Christian Doctrine
drafts.subtitle: Augustine's handbook for reading Scripture well, and the book behind "the gold of Egypt"
drafts.body:
St. Augustine wrote On Christian Doctrine (De doctrina christiana) for anyone who has to read the Bible and then explain it to others. It is a teacher's handbook, and a surprisingly practical one. Its four books ask two questions: how do we find the meaning of Scripture, and how do we share it once we have found it?

Why read it. Book I sets the goal for everything that follows: all Scripture aims at the love of God and of neighbour. Books II and III deal with words and signs: languages, translations, figures of speech, and the famous counsel that whatever is true in pagan learning belongs to God and may be put to Christian use. Book IV is Augustine the former professor of rhetoric, explaining how a Christian should teach, delight, and move a listener.

Where to begin. Start with Book II, chapters 18 to 42. It is about an hour of reading and connects directly to this week's essay. Then go back to Book I for the foundation. Save Book IV for when you are preparing to teach or write.

Which edition. For a free, reliable English text, use James Shaw's translation in the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers (1887), linked below. It is older English but clear. If you buy a modern translation, check that it includes all four books.

One question to carry. If every reading of Scripture must build up love, how should that change the way we read a passage we find difficult?

Prefer a print copy? [BOOKSHOP LINK – pending affiliate verification]

Some links are affiliate links; if you buy through them, the library earns a small commission at no extra cost to you.

Whoever, then, thinks that he understands the Holy Scriptures, or any part of them, but puts such an interpretation upon them as does not tend to build up this twofold love of God and our neighbor, does not yet understand them as he ought.

— St. Augustine, On Christian Doctrine, Book I, ch. 36 (§40); trans. James Shaw, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series, vol. 2 (1887)

Liturgical note. Advent is a season of listening for the Word. Augustine's little handbook is about exactly that: learning to hear Scripture rightly, so that we can receive the Word made flesh with understanding and with love.

drafts.title: What Did Augustine Mean by the Gold of Egypt?
drafts.subtitle: One image from the Exodus, and the four things it was meant to teach
drafts.body:
"Plundering the Egyptians" has become a shorthand for Christians using secular learning. The phrase is so familiar that it is easy to miss how carefully Augustine built the image. This exploration asks one narrow question: what exactly did he mean by it?

The story behind it

When the Israelites left Egypt, the Book of Exodus tells us, they asked their Egyptian neighbours for vessels of silver and gold and for clothing, and the Egyptians gave them (Exodus 3:22, 11:2, 12:35–36). Augustine was not the first to read this as a figure for learning. A century and a half earlier, Origen had written to his student Gregory that the Israelites made the vessels of the tabernacle from Egyptian gold, and that a Christian could likewise take from Greek philosophy "what may serve as a course of study or a preparation for Christianity."

Augustine took up the figure in Book II, chapter 40 of On Christian Doctrine, and gave it the form the tradition remembers. Read slowly, his paragraph makes four distinct points.

1. The gold was never theirs

The Egyptians' gold and silver, Augustine says, were things "which they did not create themselves, but dug out of the mines of God's providence which are everywhere scattered abroad." This is the heart of the image. Truth found in a pagan book is not a foreign possession that Christians acquire; it is God's, temporarily in other hands. He had already said so plainly in chapter 18: "wherever truth may be found, it belongs to his Master."

2. They took it by command

The Israelites did this "not doing this on their own authority, but by the command of God." Augustine is not licensing grabbing whatever seems useful. The taking is ordered to God's purpose: the Christian should "devote [it] to their proper use in preaching the gospel."

3. Gold, and also garments

The image is not only about ideas. Augustine adds the Egyptians' clothing: "human institutions such as are adapted to that intercourse with men which is indispensable in this life." Grammar, writing, law, the ordinary arts of a civilized life: these too can be taken over and put to Christian use. He then names those who had done it, from Cyprian and Lactantius to Hilary, and, before all of them, Moses, who "was learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians" (Acts 7:22).

4. The gold can also make a calf

Here is the point most often left out. The same Exodus story includes the golden calf. Origen had already warned that "not many take from Egypt only the useful," and that some "from their Greek studies, produce heretical notions, and set them up, like the golden calf."

Augustine knew this from his own life. In the Confessions he describes reading the books of the Platonists and using the same image of himself:

I set my mind upon the gold which Thou willedst Thy people to take from Egypt, seeing Thine it was, wheresoever it were.

But in the next breath he adds that he did not set his mind "on the idols of Egypt, whom they served with Thy gold." Gold carried out of Egypt can furnish the tabernacle or be melted into an idol. The metal is the same; the use is what differs. That is why, directly after the gold of Egypt, On Christian Doctrine turns to humility and the Passover.

So what did he mean?

In short: truth is God's wherever it turns up; Christians may take it, under obedience, for God's service; this includes the ordinary arts as well as philosophy; and the reader must watch that the gold is not turned into a new idol.

It is worth adding that Augustine offers this reading of Exodus "without prejudice to any other interpretation that may be as good, or better." It is a Father's counsel, widely loved, not a definition of faith.

For the larger question of why a Christian would read the pagans at all, see this week's essay. For the book this image comes from, see this week's Book of the Week on On Christian Doctrine.

drafts.title: Does Reading an Author Mean Endorsing Him?
drafts.subtitle: St. Paul quotes a pagan poet, and St. Thomas explains why that is not a compliment to paganism
drafts.body:
Many readers carry a quiet worry: if I read this author, quote him, or recommend him, am I signing off on everything he believed? The worry is understandable. But the Catholic tradition has a clear and useful distinction here, and one passage of St. Thomas Aquinas states it better than any other.

Paul in Athens

The example Thomas chooses comes from Scripture itself. When St. Paul preached on the Areopagus, he quoted a Greek poet to his pagan audience. In the words Thomas cites: "As some also of your own poets said: For we are also His offspring" (Acts 17:28). The poet, Aratus, was no Christian. Paul quoted him anyway, because on this point he was right.

Thomas's distinction

In the first question of the Summa Theologiae, Thomas asks whether sacred doctrine argues at all. In answering, he sorts the authorities a theologian may cite into three kinds, and gives each a different weight:

Nevertheless, sacred doctrine makes use of these authorities as extrinsic and probable arguments; but properly uses the authority of the canonical Scriptures as an incontrovertible proof, and the authority of the doctors of the Church as one that may properly be used, yet merely as probable.

— St. Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I, q. 1, a. 8, ad 2

So there are three levels:

  1. Philosophers (Aristotle, Plato, Aratus): used "in those questions in which they were able to know the truth by natural reason," as outside, probable support.
  2. The doctors of the Church (Augustine, Jerome, and the rest): used properly, but still "merely as probable."
  3. The canonical Scriptures: "an incontrovertible proof."

Thomas then gives the reason: "our faith rests upon the revelation made to the apostles and prophets who wrote the canonical books, and not on the revelations (if any such there are) made to other doctors."

Notice what this does. Citing Aristotle on a question of natural reason does not make Aristotle an authority on the Trinity. And even citing a saint does not make his every opinion binding. Each source is weighed for what it can actually bear.

Agreeing in part

St. Justin Martyr, writing in the second century, describes the same distinction from the side of a convert. He had loved Plato. Why, then, become a Christian?

not because the teachings of Plato are different from those of Christ, but because they are not in all respects similar

— St. Justin Martyr, Second Apology, ch. 13

"Not in all respects similar" is exactly the reader's position. We can hold that Plato saw something true about the good, and also that he was wrong about other things, without contradiction.

Augustine shows what this looks like in practice. In Book VIII of The City of God he can write, "It is evident that none come nearer to us than the Platonists." Yet the surrounding books are an extended argument with those same Platonists about worship and mediation. Praise and disagreement sit in the same pages, because he is judging each claim, not the man as a whole.

A working rule

Put together, the tradition suggests a simple habit:

  • Ask what kind of question this is. Is the author speaking where natural reason, observation, or experience can reach? Then his argument can be weighed on its merits.
  • Weigh the source for what it can bear. A philosopher's argument, a saint's opinion, and a text of Scripture do not carry the same weight, and Thomas says so explicitly.
  • Receive the true and set aside the rest. Augustine's counsel is to recognize and acknowledge the truth "even in their religious literature," and to "reject the figments of superstition."

None of this means every book is wise to read at every moment. Prudence about what to read, and when, is a real virtue, and a confessor or spiritual director may counsel a particular person differently. But reading an author, and even learning from him, is not the same as endorsing him.

For why the early Church thought this kind of reading was worth the trouble, see this week's essay, "Why Would a Christian Read the Pagans?"

Dear friends,

Advent is underway, and many of us are looking for gifts that last longer than the wrapping. Here are eight Catholic classics already in the Bibliotheca Catholica reading room. For each one, the free text on the site comes first. If you prefer a print copy for someone under the tree, a Bookshop.org link will go here once our affiliate shop is verified, and Bibliotheca Business is building a matching gift list (URL to come) so you can find them in one place.

Some links below are marked as affiliate placeholders. When they go live, if you buy through them, the library earns a small commission at no extra cost to you.

drafts.title: If God Governs All Things, Why Do My Choices Matter?
drafts.subtitle: Boethius in prison, Augustine against the fatalists, and the dignity of being a real cause
drafts.body:
Most of us have had the thought at some point, usually late at night. If God already knows everything that will happen, and if nothing escapes His providence, then what difference does my choice make? Why agonize over a decision, or pray about it, if the outcome is already in His hands?

The question can lead in two bad directions. One is a quiet fatalism: whatever will be, will be, so effort and prayer are a kind of theatre. The other is to shrink God down to make room for us, imagining Him as a spectator who set the world going and now waits to see what we do. The Catholic tradition refuses both. It holds, at the same time, that God governs all things and that our choices are truly ours. The writers who have helped me most to see how those fit together are a condemned man in a sixth-century prison, a bishop arguing with Cicero, and a friar who gave the whole matter a single phrase: the dignity of causality.

A man waiting for execution

In the early sixth century, the Roman statesman Boethius was imprisoned on charges he insisted were false; he was put to death in 524. While he awaited execution, he wrote The Consolation of Philosophy, a dialogue between himself and Lady Philosophy, who visits his cell.

Boethius begins where many of us begin when life goes wrong: with the feeling that the world is ruled by luck. Lady Philosophy lets Fortune speak for herself:

This is my art, this the game I never cease to play. I turn the wheel that spins. I delight to see the high come down and the low ascend.

— Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy, Book II

If Fortune were the last word, there would be little to say. But Philosophy leads him past the wheel to something steadier. In Book IV she distinguishes two ways of looking at the same order of events:

Providence is the Divine reason itself, seated in the Supreme Being, which disposes all things; fate is the disposition inherent in all things which move, through which providence joins all things in their proper order.

— Consolation, Book IV

What we experience as a chain of causes unfolding in time, one thing after another, God sees as a single, ordered whole. Boethius compares it to a craftsman who forms the whole design in his mind before carrying it out step by step. The steps are real. But they are not random, and they are not the whole story.

"We embrace both"

A century earlier, St. Augustine had faced the same question in a sharper form. Cicero, the great Roman orator, had argued that if God foreknows everything, then everything happens by necessity and the will cannot be free. To save freedom, Cicero was willing to deny that the future could be known at all.

Augustine thought that was too high a price. In Book V of The City of God he answers:

Therefore we are by no means compelled, either, retaining the prescience of God, to take away the freedom of the will, or, retaining the freedom of the will, to deny that He is prescient of future things, which is impious. But we embrace both. We faithfully and sincerely confess both. The former, that we may believe well; the latter, that we may live well.

— St. Augustine, The City of God, Book V, ch. 10

That last line is worth slowing down for. We confess God's foreknowledge "that we may believe well": a God who did not know the future would not be God. We confess free will "that we may live well": without it, repentance, effort, and love would be meaningless. Augustine does not claim to have dissolved every difficulty. He refuses to buy a tidy answer by giving up either truth.

The dignity of causality

St. Thomas Aquinas, writing in the thirteenth century, offers a way of seeing why the two truths need not compete. When he asks whether God governs everything directly, he answers that God has the plan of all things, down to the smallest, in His own mind. But in carrying it out, God works through creatures:

He governs things inferior by superior, not on account of any defect in His power, but by reason of the abundance of His goodness; so that the dignity of causality is imparted even to creatures.

— St. Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I, q. 22, a. 3

God does not use us because He needs help. He uses us because He is generous. He wants creatures to share in His work, as real causes and not as puppets. In the next article Thomas adds that providence does not make everything necessary. God has "prepared for some things necessary causes, so that they happen of necessity; for others contingent causes, that they may happen by contingency." Our free choices belong to that second kind. Providence does not override them. It is the reason they exist.

Seen this way, the question "If God governs all things, why do my choices matter?" turns inside out. My choices matter because God governs all things, and has chosen to govern part of the world through me.

What this changes

If that is right, it changes how we pray and how we act.

Prayer is not wasted. At the very end of the Consolation, Lady Philosophy says plainly: "Our hopes and prayers also are not fixed on God in vain, and when they are rightly directed cannot fail of effect." Prayer is one of the ways God has chosen to make us causes in His providence.

Responsibility is real. The final sentence of the book is not comfort but a charge: "Great is the necessity of righteousness laid upon you if ye will not hide it from yourselves, seeing that all your actions are done before the eyes of a Judge who seeth all things." If my choices are real, so is my accountability for them.

Anxiety can loosen. Trusting providence is not the same as being passive. It means doing the next right thing with care, and then leaving the outcome to the One who sees the whole design.

Boethius was not rescued. His conviction that providence ruled did not get him out of prison, and he never claimed it would. What it gave him was a place to stand.

What the Church teaches, and what this essay argues

Church teaching. The Catechism of the Catholic Church (paragraphs 302 to 314) teaches that God guides all creation by His providence. It also teaches that God makes use of His creatures' cooperation, not out of weakness but out of goodness. He gives them the dignity of acting on their own and of being causes, and He gives human beings the power to share freely in His providence. It teaches, too, that God is in no way the cause of moral evil, though He permits it and can draw good from it.

Theological explanation. Boethius's distinction between providence and fate, and Thomas's account of secondary causes, are explanations offered by great Christian thinkers. They are widely respected and deeply traditional. They are not themselves definitions of faith.

This essay's argument. The practical conclusions above, that prayer is one of the ways God makes us causes, and that trust in providence should loosen anxiety without breeding passivity, are my own application. They are offered for your reflection.

Where to start

Read Book IV, prose 6 and Book V, prose 6 of the Consolation. Together they take about half an hour. Then read City of God Book V, chapters 9 and 10. This week's Book of the Week introduces the Consolation as a whole.

drafts.subtitle: Boethius's prison dialogue on fortune, happiness, and providence
drafts.body:
Boethius was a Roman statesman and a Christian. He was imprisoned on charges he denied, wrote this book while awaiting death, and was executed in 524. In it Lady Philosophy visits his cell and talks him back from despair. The book alternates prose and verse, and it was among the most widely read books of the Middle Ages.

Why read it. It takes the oldest complaint seriously: why do the wicked prosper and the good suffer? And it answers by reasoning, step by step, from Fortune's wheel to true happiness to God's providence.

Where to begin. Start with Book II, where Fortune defends herself. Then go on to Book IV, prose 6, on providence and fate, and Book V, prose 6, on eternity and free will. These connect directly to this week's essay and explorations.

Which edition. The library's free text is H. R. James's translation (1897), which renders the verse as verse. Its English is older but clear. If you buy a modern translation, choose one that keeps the poems.

One question to carry. Lady Philosophy says no one can take from you what is truly yours. What, in your life, could Fortune not take away?

drafts.title: What Did Boethius Mean by an "Eternal Present"?
drafts.subtitle: Why God's knowing the future is more like seeing than predicting
drafts.body:
One of the hardest knots in Christian thought is this: if God knows today what I will choose tomorrow, how can tomorrow's choice be free? Boethius, writing in prison in the sixth century, untied it with one idea, which he puts in the mouth of Lady Philosophy in the last book of The Consolation of Philosophy. This exploration asks only what that idea is.

Eternity is not a very long time

We usually picture eternity as time that never ends: an endless line running forward. Boethius says that is the wrong picture. His definition:

Now, eternity is the possession of endless life whole and perfect at a single moment.

— Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy, Book V, prose 6

Everything in time, he explains, lives one moment at a time: "To-morrow's state it grasps not yet, while it has already lost yesterday's." Even a world that had no beginning and no end, as some philosophers imagined, would still be living moment by moment. It would be endless, but not eternal. Hence his neat distinction: "God indeed is eternal, but the world everlasting."

God does not move along the line of time at all. He possesses His whole life at once.

Knowledge "of a moment that never passes"

If that is what God's life is like, then His knowledge is like it too. God does not look ahead to our future, as a forecaster does. He sees all times as present:

thou wilt more rightly deem it not foreknowledge as of something future, but knowledge of a moment that never passes.

— Consolation, Book V, prose 6

Boethius even draws a lesson from the word itself. What God has is better called "not prevision, but providence," because "its outlook embraces all things as from some lofty height."

Seeing does not force

Now the key step. Philosophy asks Boethius a simple question: when you watch something happen, does your watching make it happen?

Why, then, dost thou insist that the things which are surveyed by the Divine eye are involved in necessity, whereas clearly men impose no necessity on things which they see? Does the act of vision add any necessity to the things which thou seest before thy eyes?

"Assuredly not," he answers.

She then gives an example. When you look out and see, at the same moment, a man walking and the sun rising, you take in both at a glance. Yet you know the difference between them: you judge "the former voluntary, the latter necessary action." Seeing both at once does not turn the man's walk into something as fixed as the sunrise.

So it is with God. His vision takes in all things in His eternal present, but it "changes not the natures and properties of things." What is free is seen as free, and it remains free.

What the idea does, and does not, do

The eternal present answers one specific worry: that God's knowing our choices makes them unfree. It shows that knowledge as such, whether ours of the present or God's of all time, does not compel.

It does not, by itself, answer every question about grace, predestination, and freedom. Later theologians, St. Thomas Aquinas among them, took up Boethius's definition and built on it, and they debated the deeper questions for centuries. Boethius's image is a starting point, not the whole conversation.

It is also worth being clear that the eternal present is a philosophical explanation. What the Church teaches as a matter of faith is that God knows all things, governs all things by His providence, and that human beings are truly free (see the Catechism, paragraphs 302 to 314). Boethius offers one of the most helpful ways ever found of seeing how those truths fit together.

For the larger question of why our choices matter at all, see this week's essay, "If God Governs All Things, Why Do My Choices Matter?"

drafts.title: Is "Everything Happens for a Reason" a Catholic Idea?
drafts.subtitle: What the saying gets right, what it gets wrong, and what the Church actually says
drafts.body:
It is one of the most common things people say at funerals and in hospital corridors: "Everything happens for a reason." It is usually meant kindly. But Catholics who hear it can feel two things at once: that it is true, and that something about it is badly off. This exploration asks one narrow question: in what sense, if any, is the saying Catholic?

What it gets right: nothing falls outside providence

The Church teaches that God's providence is not vague or distant. The Catechism (paragraphs 302 to 305) says that God guides His creation toward its perfection, that His care reaches from the least things to the great events of history, and that Christ invites us to trust our heavenly Father with even our smallest needs. In that sense nothing is outside God's knowledge or care. Nothing "just happens" in a world God has abandoned.

What it gets wrong: evil is not made good

The saying goes wrong when it suggests that every event, including sin and cruelty, is itself good or directly willed by God. The Catechism is careful here (paragraphs 311 to 312). God is in no way the cause of moral evil. He permits it, out of respect for the freedom of His creatures, and He knows how to bring good from it. But the evil itself never becomes a good.

St. Augustine put the principle in a sentence the Catechism itself cites:

For the Almighty God, who, as even the heathen acknowledge, has supreme power over all things, being Himself supremely good, would never permit the existence of anything evil among His works, if He were not so omnipotent and good that He can bring good even out of evil.

— St. Augustine, Enchiridion, ch. 11

Notice the shape of the claim. God permits evil. He brings good out of it. That is very different from saying the evil was the good, or was sent so that the good could happen.

St. Thomas Aquinas gives a sober example. A provider who cares for the whole, he says, will allow some defects in the parts, "for if all evil were prevented, much good would be absent from the universe." Then he adds: "there would be no patience of martyrs if there were no tyrannical persecution." The martyr's patience is a real good. The persecution remains a real evil. God permits the second without approving it, and draws out the first.

What we usually cannot say: the reason

There is a second problem with the saying. It implies that we can know, or should be able to name, the reason. The Catechism says the opposite (paragraph 314): the ways of God's providence are often unknown to us, and we will fully understand them only when we see God face to face.

This matters pastorally. Telling a grieving person "it happened for a reason" can sound like a demand that they find the reason now, or accept one we have invented for them. The Catholic answer is more modest. God is at work, and He can bring good even from this. But we may not see how in this life.

A better way to say it

The Catechism gathers several saints on this point (paragraph 313). Among them is a line from Julian of Norwich, the fourteenth-century English anchoress. After asking why God did not simply prevent sin, she records this answer:

It behoved that there should be sin; but all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well.

— Julian of Norwich, Revelations of Divine Love, ch. XXVII

Julian's showings are a private revelation. Catholics are free to draw on them but are not bound to them. Yet her words are close to what the Church means. They do not claim that sin is good, or that we can see the reason. They say that God will set all things right.

So instead of "everything happens for a reason," a Catholic might say: nothing is beyond God's care, and He can bring good even out of this. It is less tidy. It is also truer, and it does not ask the suffering to pretend.

drafts.title: How Do We Know What Happened?
drafts.subtitle: Eusebius, Bede, and a Jesuit scholar on reading Christian history as evidence
drafts.body:
Christianity is a religion of events. The Creed names a Roman governor. The Gospels give us places, rulers, and the names of witnesses. The faith does not float above history; it claims that certain things really happened.

That is why Christians have always cared about evidence. If the faith rests on events, it matters how we know about them. It also matters how we read the many later stories that have gathered around those events: chronicles, saints' lives, legends, and pious traditions. Some are history of the first order. Some are devotion dressed as history. A thoughtful Catholic reader needs to tell the difference without becoming either credulous or cynical.

Three writers in the library, spread across sixteen centuries, show how.

Eusebius: the first to walk the road

Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339) set out to write a history of the Church from the apostles to his own day. He knew he was doing something new, and he said so:

since I am the first to enter upon the subject, I am attempting to traverse as it were a lonely and untrodden path.

— Eusebius, Church History, Book I, ch. 1

Eusebius did not have a tradition of Church historians to rely on. What he had were "brief fragments": letters, lists of bishops, and earlier writings. He describes them beautifully: "From afar they raise their voices like torches." His method, which he follows throughout the book, was to gather those voices, quote them, and let the reader see the sources for himself. Much of what we know about the first three Christian centuries survives only because Eusebius copied it.

Bede: naming his witnesses

Four centuries later, in a monastery in the north of England, the Venerable Bede finished his Ecclesiastical History of the English People. He opens it with a preface to King Ceolwulf that is, in effect, a list of sources.

He explains why he is giving one: "to the end that I may remove all occasion of doubting what I have written." Then he names names. His "principal authority and aid" was Abbot Albinus of Canterbury. A London priest named Nothelm searched the papal archives in Rome and brought back letters of Pope Gregory. Bishop Daniel of the West Saxons sent written information. For events in Northumbria, Bede relied not on one man but on "the faithful testimony of innumerable witnesses," as well as his own knowledge.

Bede closes the preface with a request that every honest historian could make:

And I humbly entreat the reader, that if he shall find in these our writings anything not delivered according to the truth, he will not lay the blame of it on me, for, as the true rule of history requires, withholding nothing, I have laboured to commit to writing such things as I could gather from common report, for the instruction of posterity.

— Bede, Ecclesiastical History, Preface

Notice two things. First, Bede is transparent: he tells you where his information came from, so you can weigh it. Second, he is modest: he reports what his sources told him, including miracle stories, and he does not claim more certainty than he has. (This week's short exploration looks at his preface more closely.)

Delehaye: history and hagiography

Twelve centuries after Bede, a Belgian Jesuit named Hippolyte Delehaye took up a harder question. He belonged to the Bollandists, a society of scholars devoted to studying the lives of the saints. He wrote a short book in French, Légendes hagiographiques, which was translated into English in 1907 as The Legends of the Saints. It begins with a distinction:

The point to be emphasised from the first is the distinction between hagiography and history. The work of the hagiographer may be historical, but it is not necessarily so.

— Hippolyte Delehaye, S.J., The Legends of the Saints, ch. I

A saint's life written to edify the faithful is a work of devotion. It may preserve real history, or it may be closer to a poem or a legend. Delehaye knew that some devout readers would hear this as an attack on the saints. He answered that the opposite was true. People accused careful scholars of rationalism, he wrote, "as though in questions of fact it were not above all things essential to weigh the evidence." And sorting the reliable from the unreliable does not diminish the saints:

To give assistance in detecting materials of inferior workmanship is not to deny the excellence of what remains, and it is to the ultimate advantage of the harvest to point out the tares that have sometimes become mingled with the wheat to a most disconcerting extent.

— Delehaye, The Legends of the Saints, Author's Introduction

Four questions to ask of any source

Taken together, these writers suggest a few plain questions for reading any historical claim, whether in an old chronicle or a modern article:

  1. Who says so? Eusebius quotes his sources. Bede names his.
  2. How could they know? Were they eyewitnesses, or did they learn it from others? Bede distinguishes what he gathered from documents, from informants, and "from common report."
  3. When was it written? A letter from the time carries a different weight from a story written down centuries later.
  4. What kind of writing is it? As Delehaye insists, a sermon, a legend, and a chronicle are not trying to do the same thing.

These questions are not hostile to faith. They are what it looks like to take the truth seriously.

Why this matters now

These are not only questions for scholars. Every week, quotations attributed to saints circulate online with no source at all. Some are genuine. Many are paraphrases that have hardened into quotations, and some were never said. Stories about the early Church are retold with confidence and without a footnote.

The library exists partly to help with exactly this: to put the texts themselves within reach, so that readers can check what a Father or a saint actually wrote. Eusebius and Bede would recognize the instinct. Both wanted their readers to be able to see where the story came from. Delehaye wanted the same, and he thought the saints had nothing to fear from it.

What the Church teaches, and what this essay argues

Church teaching. The Second Vatican Council's Dei Verbum (no. 19) teaches that the Church firmly holds the historical character of the four Gospels. They faithfully hand on what Jesus really did and taught. The Council also notes that the evangelists selected and arranged material from what had been handed down, while always telling the honest truth about Jesus. The faith is bound to real events.

What is not Church teaching. The particular details of later chronicles and saints' legends are not, as such, articles of faith. Delehaye's book is a scholar's work, not a magisterial document, and Bede's and Eusebius's judgments are those of historians. They can be right or wrong on a given point.

This essay's argument. The four questions above are my own summary, drawn from these writers, of a sensible way to read. They are offered as a practical aid, not as a rule the Church has laid down.

Where to start

Read Bede's preface; it takes ten minutes. Then read Book I, chapter 1 of Eusebius. Delehaye's Author's Introduction is short and is a good next step. This week's Book of the Week introduces Bede's History as a whole.

drafts.title: Book of the Week: Bede's Ecclesiastical History of the English People
drafts.subtitle: How the Faith came to England, told by a monk who named his sources
drafts.body:
St. Bede the Venerable, a monk of Jarrow and a Doctor of the Church, finished his Ecclesiastical History in 731. Across five books he tells how the Gospel reached Britain and the English. His story runs from Julius Caesar's arrival, through Pope Gregory's mission to Kent, to the saints, kings, and councils of his own day.

Why read it. It is a history full of saints: Augustine of Canterbury, Aidan, Hilda, and Cuthbert. It is also a model of careful method, because Bede tells the reader where his information came from. And it is full of memorable scenes, such as King Oswald raising a wooden cross before battle.

Where to begin. Start with the short preface, where Bede lists his sources. Then read Book I, chapters 23 to 26, on Augustine's mission, and Book III, chapters 1 to 6, on Oswald and Aidan.

Which edition. The library's free text is A. M. Sellar's revised translation (1907). It has a helpful introduction, a life of Bede, and notes that identify places and people. That makes it easy to follow.

One question to carry. Bede says history moves the reader "to imitate that which is good." Which figure in the story would you most like to imitate?

drafts.title: Is a Saint's Legend the Same as History?
drafts.subtitle: What the word "legend" first meant, and how a Jesuit scholar taught us to read one
drafts.body:
The library holds a great many saints' lives, from Jacobus de Voragine's Golden Legend to Butler's and Baring-Gould's collections. Readers sometimes ask, a little anxiously: are these stories true? Is it irreverent to notice, as Delehaye himself did, that the legend of St. Dymphna echoes the old folk tale of "the ass's skin"? This exploration takes one narrow question, what a legend actually is, and answers it through one source: Hippolyte Delehaye's The Legends of the Saints (English translation, 1907).

"Legend" first meant "what is to be read"

We hear "legend" and think "made up." Delehaye points out that the word began somewhere else entirely. In its original sense, he writes, the legend "is the history that has to be read, legenda, on the feast of a saint." It was simply the reading for the day, the account of a martyr's passion or a confessor's life, "without reference to its historical value."

By the thirteenth century, he notes, the Golden Legend had made the word cover every kind of saint's life. So when a medieval reader called a book a "legend," he was not confessing that it was fiction. He was naming its use in prayer.

Two ingredients

To avoid confusion, Delehaye then narrows the word. In his book, "legend" will mean only "stories or incidents unauthenticated by history." And he explains how such stories arise. A legend, he says, presupposes "an historical fact as basis or pretext." That fact "may either be developed or disfigured by popular imagination." The two ingredients can be mixed "in very unequal proportions." Depending on whether fact or fiction predominates, "the narrative may be classed as history or as legend."

This is the key idea. Most saints' lives are not simply true or simply false. They are a real person, often a real martyrdom or a real holy life, to which imagination has added more or less ornament over time.

Hagiography is not trying to be history

Delehaye's most important distinction comes at the start of his book:

The point to be emphasised from the first is the distinction between hagiography and history. The work of the hagiographer may be historical, but it is not necessarily so.

— Delehaye, The Legends of the Saints, ch. I

A saint's life is written, as he says, to inspire devotion and edify the faithful. It can take "any literary form suitable to the glorification of the saints," from an official record to "a poetical composition of the most exuberant character wholly detached from reality." To ask of every saint's life whether it is accurate history is a little like asking whether a hymn is a newspaper report.

So how should we read them?

Delehaye's answer is neither "believe everything" nor "believe nothing."

  • Weigh the evidence for each story. Whether a given detail is historical is, in his words, "a point to be determined in each individual case."
  • Don't confuse doubting a legend with doubting a saint. He complains of readers who think that questioning a biographer means "attacking the saint himself."
  • Value what is genuine all the more. The early accounts written by eyewitnesses, he says, "deserve our fullest admiration and respect," and that is exactly why they must be distinguished from later embellishments.

It is worth adding a clear line. The Church venerates the saints and celebrates their feasts. But the particular details of a medieval saint's life are not, as such, part of the Catholic faith. Delehaye himself was a Jesuit priest who spent his life in this work, and he saw careful sorting as a service to the saints, not a threat. (That is a description of his scholarly position, not a statement of Church teaching.)

For the wider question of how to weigh historical evidence, see this week's essay, "How Do We Know What Happened?"

drafts.title: How Did Bede Know?
drafts.subtitle: Reading the preface, and one chapter, of the Ecclesiastical History for the way Bede signals his sources
drafts.body:
The Venerable Bede wrote about events that happened, in some cases, a century or more before he was born. How could he know them? This exploration does not try to judge every story in the Ecclesiastical History. It asks something narrower: how does Bede tell us where his information comes from, so that we can judge for ourselves?

The preface: a list of sources

Bede dedicates the History to King Ceolwulf of Northumbria. Partway through the dedication he turns to the question of sources, and gives his reason for doing so: "to the end that I may remove all occasion of doubting what I have written, both from yourself and other readers or hearers of this history, I will take care briefly to show you from what authors I chiefly learned the same."

What follows is, in effect, a map of his evidence, region by region:

  • Kent and the mission of Pope Gregory's disciples: Abbot Albinus of Canterbury, sending material through the London priest Nothelm, "either in writing, or by word of mouth."
  • Papal letters: Nothelm went to Rome and "searched into the archives of the Holy Roman Church," bringing back "some epistles of the blessed Pope Gregory, and other popes."
  • The West Saxons, South Saxons, and the Isle of Wight: Bishop Daniel, "who is still living," who sent him information in writing.
  • The Mercians and East Saxons: "the brethren of the monastery" founded by Cedd and Ceadda, at Lastingham.
  • The East Angles: "the writings and tradition of former men," and "the account of the most reverend Abbot Esi."
  • Lindsey: "the letters of the most reverend prelate Cynibert, or by word of mouth from other persons of good credit."
  • Northumbria, his own region: "not on the authority of any one man, but by the faithful testimony of innumerable witnesses," besides "what I had of my own knowledge."

That is a remarkable thing for an eighth-century monk to have done. He separates written documents from oral reports, names his informants, notes which are still alive, and distinguishes what he knows firsthand.

The same habits inside the stories

Bede keeps these signals going in the narrative itself. Take Book III, chapter 2, the story of King Oswald raising a wooden cross before the battle at Heavenfield. Read it closely, and you can see three different kinds of claim:

  1. What he has been told: "Then, we are told, that the cross being made in haste... the king himself... laid hold of it and held it upright with both his hands." The phrase "we are told" marks a report handed down to him.
  2. What can still be seen: "The place is shown to this day, and held in much veneration." That is a present-day fact his readers could check.
  3. A named, living witness: For a healing at the cross, he names the man: "One of the brothers of the same church of Hagulstald, whose name is Bothelm, and who is still living."

Bede believed in miracles, and he reports them without embarrassment. But he does not present a story about a battle long ago in the same way as a cure he could attribute to a man his readers might meet. He lets the reader see the difference.

Bede's own standard

The preface ends with a phrase historians still quote. Bede asks the reader not to blame him for any errors, "for, as the true rule of history requires, withholding nothing, I have laboured to commit to writing such things as I could gather from common report, for the instruction of posterity."

"Common report" is an honest admission. Some of what he records is what people said. By telling us so, Bede gives us the tools to weigh it.

What this does, and doesn't, settle

Knowing Bede's sources does not prove every story true. A named informant can be mistaken, and a report can grow in the retelling. But it shows a historian who wanted to be checked, and that is the first mark of one worth trusting.

For the larger question of how to read historical claims, see this week's essay, "How Do We Know What Happened?"

drafts.title: What Do Catholics Mean by "Tradition"?
drafts.subtitle: Not nostalgia, not a second Bible, but the living handing-on of the Gospel
drafts.body:
"Tradition" is one of those words Catholics use constantly and explain rarely. To some people it suggests nostalgia: a fondness for the way things used to be done. To others it suggests a second, secret source of doctrine alongside the Bible. Neither is what the Church means. At heart the word means a handing-on, and what it describes is simple. Christ gave the Gospel to the apostles, and the apostles handed it on, by their preaching and their writing, to those who came after them.

This essay looks at what the Church teaches about Tradition, and at three early witnesses in the library who help us see it at work.

What the Church teaches

The clearest modern statement is the Second Vatican Council's constitution Dei Verbum, which the Catechism follows closely (paragraphs 75 to 83).

Tradition comes from the apostles. The Council teaches that the apostles handed on the Gospel in two ways. Some was handed on orally, by their preaching, their example, and the observances they established. Some was handed on in writing, by those who, under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, set the message of salvation down in the books of the New Testament. To keep the Gospel whole and alive, the apostles left bishops as their successors.

Scripture and Tradition belong together. Dei Verbum describes Scripture and Tradition as flowing from the same divine wellspring and tending toward the same end. Scripture is the word of God written under the inspiration of the Spirit. Tradition hands on that same word of God, entrusted to the apostles, to their successors. The Church therefore does not draw her certainty about everything revealed from Scripture alone, and both are to be received with the same reverence.

The teaching office serves the word. The task of authentically interpreting the word of God belongs to the Church's teaching office. But the Council adds at once that this office is not above the word of God. It serves it, teaching only what has been handed on.

The apostles themselves pointed to it. Dei Verbum recalls that the apostles, handing on what they had received, warned the faithful to hold fast to the traditions they had learned, whether by word of mouth or by letter. St. Paul's words, as St. Basil quoted them in the fourth century, are "Hold fast the traditions which ye have been taught whether by word, or our Epistle" (2 Thessalonians 2:15). The New Testament does not present itself as the only way the Gospel was handed on.

Tradition grows in understanding. Dei Verbum also says that the Tradition from the apostles develops in the Church with the help of the Holy Spirit. This is not by adding new revelation. It is by a growth in understanding of what was handed down.

Irenaeus: you can check it

In the second century, St. Irenaeus of Lyons (c. 130–202) was writing against Gnostic teachers who claimed to possess secret doctrines passed on privately from the apostles. His answer was an appeal to something public:

It is within the power of all, therefore, in every Church, who may wish to see the truth, to contemplate clearly the tradition of the apostles manifested throughout the whole world.

— St. Irenaeus, Against Heresies, Book III, ch. 3

If the apostles had secret teachings, he argues, they would have given them to the men they entrusted with the churches. And those men are known by name, in an unbroken line. He gives his own example. As a young man he had seen St. Polycarp, who had been taught by apostles, and who died, Irenaeus says, "having always taught the things which he had learned from the apostles, and which the Church has handed down, and which alone are true."

For Irenaeus, then, Tradition is the opposite of secret. It is the public, continuous teaching of the churches founded by the apostles, which anyone can examine.

Vincent: growth without change of meaning

In the fifth century, St. Vincent of Lérins (d. c. 445) faced a different question. If the faith is handed on unchanged, can there be any progress in it at all? He answers yes, and offers an image that has never been bettered:

The growth of religion in the soul must be analogous to the growth of the body, which, though in process of years it is developed and attains its full size, yet remains still the same.

— St. Vincent of Lérins, Commonitory, ch. 23

A child and the grown man are the same person, Vincent says. Nothing appears in the adult that was not already present, in some way, in the child. So with doctrine. The Church's understanding deepens and its expression becomes fuller, but it does not turn into something else. (This week's short exploration looks at Vincent's more famous rule, and at what it can and cannot settle.)

Newman: the long view

In the nineteenth century, John Henry Newman took up Vincent's image and spent a whole book testing it against the history of the Church. His Essay on the Development of Christian Doctrine (1845) proposed ways of telling a faithful development from a corruption. By the time the book was printed, he had been received into the Catholic Church: a postscript explains that, while it was in the press, he became convinced of "the truth of the conclusion to which the discussion leads." This week's Book of the Week introduces it.

Tradition and traditions

One more distinction matters. The Catechism (paragraph 83) distinguishes the apostolic Tradition from the many theological, disciplinary, liturgical, and devotional traditions that have grown up in local churches over time. These smaller traditions are particular ways in which the great Tradition is expressed. Under the guidance of the Church's teaching office, they can be kept, adapted, or even set aside.

So when a Catholic says "Tradition," he should not mean every custom he grew up with. He means the faith of the apostles, handed on and kept whole. (This week's other exploration takes up that distinction directly.)

Why it matters

This is not an abstract question. It shapes how a Catholic reads the Bible: within the living faith of the Church that first received and recognized it, not against it. It shapes how we read the Fathers: as witnesses to what was handed down, not as a collection of private opinions. And it shapes how we live with change. Some things in the Church's life do change, and should. Others cannot, because they are not ours to change. Knowing the difference between Tradition and traditions is the beginning of peace on that point.

What the Church teaches, and what this essay argues

Church teaching. Everything in the section "What the Church teaches," and the Tradition/traditions distinction, is drawn from Dei Verbum 7 to 10 and the Catechism 75 to 83. It is paraphrased rather than quoted.

The Fathers' witness. Irenaeus and Vincent are early witnesses to how the Church understood Tradition. The Catechism itself cites Irenaeus on apostolic succession. Their particular arguments and images are theirs, offered as witnesses, not as definitions.

Newman. Newman's tests for development are a theologian's proposal, widely respected and influential, but not themselves Church teaching.

This essay's framing. The opening contrast with "nostalgia" and a "second Bible" is my own way of introducing the subject.

Where to start

Read Against Heresies Book III, chapter 3. It is two pages long. Then read chapters 2 and 23 of Vincent's Commonitory. Both are available free on New Advent.

drafts.title: Tradition or Traditions?
drafts.subtitle: A distinction worth keeping, with help from St. Basil and the Catechism
drafts.body:
Catholics argue a good deal about "tradition." Often, though, they are not using the word in the same way. One person means the apostolic faith itself. Another means the way Mass was celebrated in his grandmother's parish, a particular devotion, or a custom of fasting. This exploration asks one narrow question: what is the difference between Tradition and traditions, and why does it matter?

The Catechism's distinction

The Catechism of the Catholic Church draws the line plainly in paragraph 83. The Tradition it speaks of comes from the apostles. It hands on what they received from Jesus' teaching and example and what they learned from the Holy Spirit.

That Tradition, the Catechism says, is to be distinguished from the various theological, disciplinary, liturgical, or devotional traditions that have arisen in local churches over time. These are the particular forms, suited to different places and ages, in which the great Tradition is expressed. In the light of Tradition, and under the guidance of the Church's teaching office, they can be kept, modified, or even abandoned.

So there are two levels:

  • Tradition (capital T): the apostolic deposit of faith. It is handed on with Scripture and is not ours to change.
  • traditions (small t): the many customs, forms, and practices through which that faith has been lived. They are valuable and often ancient, but they are adaptable.

Basil: unwritten customs as witnesses

St. Basil the Great, writing On the Holy Spirit in the fourth century, shows why the unwritten side of the Church's life matters. He was defending a form of words in the Church's prayer that some opponents rejected because it was not found in Scripture. His reply was to point to practices everyone already accepted without a written command:

For instance, to take the first and most general example, who is there who has taught us in writing to sign with the sign of the cross those who have trusted in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ? What writing has taught us to turn to the East at the prayer?

— St. Basil, On the Holy Spirit, ch. 27

Basil goes further. Of the beliefs and practices preserved in the Church, he says, "some we possess derived from written teaching; others we have received delivered to us 'in a mystery' by the tradition of the apostles." If we tried to reject every custom lacking written authority, he warns, "we should unintentionally injure the Gospel in its very vitals."

Basil's point is that the Church's lived practice carries the faith. Her prayers, her gestures, and the way she baptizes and worships are not decoration added to doctrine. They bear witness to it. That is exactly why the distinction matters. Some practices witness to something unchangeable, and some are particular forms of that witness.

Why the distinction helps

Keeping the two levels apart guards against two opposite mistakes.

The first mistake treats every custom as untouchable. If every inherited practice is Tradition, then any change, even one the Church herself makes, looks like betrayal. The Catechism says otherwise: small-t traditions can be modified under the guidance of the Church.

The second mistake treats the faith itself as a custom. If everything is "just tradition," then doctrine handed down from the apostles can seem as negotiable as a parish schedule. That is also wrong. The apostolic Tradition is not ours to revise.

Most real questions fall somewhere between, and that is where prudence and the judgment of the Church come in. But simply asking "Is this Tradition, or a tradition?" clears away a great deal of confusion.

A note of caution

It is not always obvious which level a particular practice belongs to. The Catechism gives the principle, not a complete list. Sorting particular cases belongs to the Church's teaching office and to careful theology, not to individual preference.

For the larger picture of what Catholics mean by Tradition, see this week's essay.

drafts.title: Book of the Week: Newman's An Essay on the Development of Christian Doctrine
drafts.subtitle: The book Newman was still printing when he became a Catholic
drafts.body:
In 1845, St. John Henry Newman was still an Anglican and was writing a book to settle a question that troubled him. Did Catholic doctrine as he saw it in his own day faithfully grow from the faith of the apostles, or had it been corrupted? While the book was at the printer, he reached his answer and joined the Catholic Church. A postscript, written afterwards, tells the story.

Why read it. Newman takes seriously the fact that doctrine has a history. He argues that a living idea unfolds over time. He then proposes seven "Notes" for telling a true development from a corruption, among them preservation of type and continuity of principles. It is still the classic treatment of the question.

Where to begin. Read the short Advertisement and Postscript first. Then read Chapter I, section 1, on how ideas develop, which ends with the famous line quoted below. Then turn to Chapter V for the seven Notes.

Which edition. The library's free text is the sixth edition. For print, the site's edition guide recommends the University of Notre Dame Press reprint.

One question to carry. Newman says a true development "changes... in order to remain the same." What in your own faith has deepened over the years without becoming something else?

drafts.title: "Everywhere, Always, by All": What Vincent's Rule Does and Doesn't Settle
drafts.subtitle: The most quoted sentence about Tradition, and Newman's honest look at its limits
drafts.body:
If you have read anything about Catholic Tradition, you have probably met the phrase: the faith is what has been believed "everywhere, always, by all." It comes from St. Vincent of Lérins, a fifth-century monk. It is often quoted as if it settled every question. This exploration asks a narrower one: what exactly did Vincent's rule claim, and what can it actually do?

The rule itself

Vincent wrote his Commonitory as a guide for telling true doctrine from heresy. In chapter 2 he states his principle:

Moreover, in the Catholic Church itself, all possible care must be taken, that we hold that faith which has been believed everywhere, always, by all.

— St. Vincent of Lérins, Commonitory, ch. 2

He immediately turns it into three tests. We follow universality "if we confess that one faith to be true, which the whole Church throughout the world confesses." We follow antiquity if we do not depart from the interpretations "notoriously held by our holy ancestors and fathers." And we follow consent if, within antiquity, we adhere to the agreed teaching "of all, or at the least of almost all priests and doctors."

Notice that small qualification: "or at the least of almost all." Even Vincent did not imagine a test requiring unanimous written testimony from every bishop who ever lived.

What the rule does well

The rule is powerful against novelty. If someone proposes a doctrine that no church held, that no early Father taught, and that the Church as a whole never confessed, Vincent's tests expose it quickly. That was his purpose: to protect the faithful from new teachings presented as ancient.

What it cannot do on its own

The difficulty comes when we try to use the rule positively, as a machine for producing a complete list of doctrines. John Henry Newman examined exactly this in the introduction to his Essay on the Development of Christian Doctrine (1845). He grants that the rule "contains a majestic truth, and offers an intelligible principle." But, he says, "its difficulty lies in applying it in particular cases. The rule is more serviceable in determining what is not, than what is Christianity."

Newman then quotes an earlier writer, in fact himself, from his Anglican years, who had already seen the problem:

what is meant by being 'taught always'? does it mean in every century, or every year, or every month? Does 'everywhere' mean in every country, or in every diocese?

— Newman, An Essay on the Development of Christian Doctrine, Introduction, quoting his Prophetical Office

The rule, that earlier writer concluded, "is not of a mathematical or demonstrative character, but moral, and requires practical judgment and good sense to apply it."

Vincent's own second step

Vincent himself did not leave the matter there. Later in the Commonitory he asks whether there can be any progress in the Church. His answer is: "Certainly; all possible progress." But it must be "real progress, not alteration of the faith." Understanding should increase "in its own kind; that is to say, in the same doctrine, in the same sense, and in the same meaning."

So Vincent's teaching has two halves. The famous rule protects what has always been believed. The principle of growth allows that what has always been believed can be understood more deeply and stated more fully over time. Newman's Essay is, in large part, an attempt to explain how to tell that kind of growth from corruption.

What this means for a reader

When you see "everywhere, always, by all" quoted, it is worth remembering three things:

  1. It is a strong test against new doctrines, which is what Vincent designed it for.
  2. It needs judgment to apply, as Vincent's own "almost all" and Newman's questions show.
  3. Vincent paired it with a principle of real growth in understanding.

It is also worth being clear about status. Vincent's rule is a Father's guide, widely respected and often cited. It is not itself a definition of faith. The Church's teaching on how Tradition is handed on and grows is set out in Dei Verbum (nos. 8 to 10).

This week's Book of the Week introduces Newman's Essay.
